text: A Lion lay asleep in the forest, his great head resting on his paws.
A timid little Mouse came upon him unexpectedly, and in her fright and haste to get away, ran across the Lion's nose.
Roused from his nap, the Lion laid his huge paw angrily on the tiny creature to kill her.
“Spare me!” begged the poor Mouse.
“Please let me go and some day I will surely repay you.”
The Lion was much amused to think that a Mouse could ever help him.
But he was generous and finally let the Mouse go.
Some days later, while stalking his prey in the forest, the Lion was caught in the toils of a hunter's net.
Unable to free himself, he filled the forest with his angry roaring.
The Mouse knew the voice and quickly found the Lion struggling in the net.
Running to one of the great ropes that bound him, she gnawed it until it parted, and soon the Lion was free.
“You laughed when I said I would repay you,” said the Mouse.
“Now you see that even a Mouse can help a Lion.”
A kindness is never wasted.
A Shepherd Boy tended his master's sheep near a dark forest, not far from the village.
One day he thought he would play a trick on the villagers.
He ran toward the village crying, “Wolf! Wolf!”
The villagers left their work and ran to the pasture to help him.
But when they arrived, the boy only laughed at them.
A few days later he cried again, “Wolf! Wolf!”
Again the villagers ran to save the sheep, and again the boy laughed.
Then a real wolf came from the forest and began to chase the sheep.
The terrified boy ran toward the village shouting louder than ever.
“Wolf! Wolf! Please come and help!” he cried.
But the villagers thought he was trying to fool them again.
No one came, and the wolf carried off many of the sheep.
Liars are not believed even when they tell the truth.
The North Wind and the Sun had a quarrel about which of them was the stronger.
While they were disputing, a traveler came along wrapped in a warm cloak.
They agreed that the one who could make the traveler take off his cloak would be called stronger.
The North Wind blew as hard as he could.
But the harder he blew, the closer the traveler wrapped his cloak around him.
At last the North Wind gave up the attempt.
Then the Sun shone out warmly from behind the clouds.
Soon the traveler felt the pleasant warmth on his shoulders.
He loosened his cloak and then took it off.
The Sun had won the contest.
Gentleness and kindness often do more than force.
One bright summer day a Grasshopper was hopping about and singing with all his heart.
An Ant passed by, carrying an ear of corn to her nest.
“Why not come and chat with me?” said the Grasshopper.
“I am helping to store food for the winter,” said the Ant.
“You should do the same.”
“Why worry about winter?” said the Grasshopper.
“We have plenty of food at present.”
But the Ant went on with her work.
When winter came, the Grasshopper found himself cold and hungry.
He saw the Ants sharing the food they had gathered in the summer.
Then the Grasshopper knew that it is best to prepare for days of need.
A Town Mouse once visited a Country Mouse who lived in a field.
The Country Mouse offered him beans, bacon, cheese, and bread.
The Town Mouse turned up his long nose at this simple country food.
“You live very poorly here,” he said.
“Come with me to town, and I will show you fine living.”
So the two mice went to the great house where the Town Mouse lived.
There they found cakes, jellies, and all sorts of dainty food.
But just as they began to eat, the door flew open.
People rushed in, and the frightened mice ran to hide.
When the room was quiet again, they crept back to the feast.
Then a cat sprang toward them, and they barely escaped with their lives.
“Good-bye,” said the Country Mouse.
“I would rather eat plain food in peace than rich food in fear.”
There was once a shoemaker who had grown so poor that he had only leather enough for one pair of shoes.
In the evening he cut out the leather and laid it on his bench.
He meant to rise early and sew the shoes in the morning.
But when he got up, the shoes stood finished on the bench.
The stitches were so neat that everyone admired them.
A customer bought the shoes at once and paid more than the usual price.
With the money, the shoemaker bought leather for two more pairs.
Again he cut the leather at night, and again the shoes were finished by morning.
This went on until the shoemaker and his wife were no longer poor.
One night they hid behind a curtain to see who helped them.
Two tiny elves came in and worked merrily until the shoes were done.
The wife said, “They have made us rich; we must thank them.”
She made little coats, shirts, stockings, and shoes for the elves.
When the elves found the gifts, they danced for joy and never came back to work.
But the shoemaker prospered in all that he did.
An old donkey had worked hard for many years, but now his strength was failing.
His master thought he was no longer useful, so the donkey ran away toward Bremen.
He hoped to become a town musician there.
On the road he met an old dog lying by the path.
“Come with me to Bremen,” said the donkey.
Soon they met a cat whose face was as sad as three rainy days.
The cat joined them, and then they found a rooster crying loudly on a gate.
The four friends walked until night came and a light shone through the forest.
They crept to the window and saw robbers eating at a table.
The donkey put his forefeet on the window, the dog climbed on his back, the cat climbed on the dog, and the rooster flew to the top.
Then they all made music at once: braying, barking, mewing, and crowing.
The robbers were so frightened that they ran into the forest.
The friends ate the supper and settled down in the house.
When a robber returned later, the animals drove him out again.
So the musicians stayed happily in the house and did not go to Bremen after all.
In old times a king's youngest daughter had a golden ball.
She loved to play with it beside a deep spring in the forest.
One day the ball fell into the water and sank out of sight.
The princess began to cry, and a frog put his head out of the spring.
“What will you give me if I bring back your ball?” asked the frog.
“Anything you want,” said the princess.
The frog asked to be her friend, to eat from her plate, and to sleep near her bed.
The princess promised, though she did not mean to keep her word.
The frog dived down and brought up the golden ball.
The princess took the ball and ran home.
That evening the frog came to the palace door and asked to come in.
The king told his daughter that a promise must be kept.
So the frog ate from her plate and stayed beside her.
At last the spell was broken, and the frog became a prince with kind eyes.
The princess learned that promises are not little things.
It was lovely summer weather in the country, and the corn stood yellow in the fields.
In a quiet corner, a mother duck sat on her nest waiting for her eggs to hatch.
At last the eggs cracked, and the little ducklings cried, “Peep, peep!”
One large egg was slower than the rest.
When it opened, out came a big, gray duckling who looked different from the others.
The other ducks pecked him and called him ugly.
The poor duckling ran away through the marshes and fields.
He passed a hard autumn and a cold winter, lonely and afraid.
When spring came, he saw three beautiful white swans on the water.
He bent his head, expecting them to drive him away.
But in the clear water he saw his own reflection.
He was no longer a gray duckling, but a beautiful swan.
The children cried, “The new one is the most beautiful of all!”
Then the young swan felt glad, but not proud.
Many years ago there was an Emperor who cared for nothing so much as new clothes.
He spent all his money on dressing well and changing his clothes every hour.
One day two strangers came to the city and said they could weave the most wonderful cloth.
They said the cloth was invisible to anyone who was foolish or unfit for his office.
The Emperor thought this cloth would show him who was wise and who was not.
He gave the strangers gold, silk, and thread, but they put nothing on the looms.
The ministers came to look, but they saw only empty frames.
Still, each one praised the beautiful colors and the splendid pattern.
At last the Emperor himself came, and he too saw nothing.
But he was afraid to seem foolish, so he praised the cloth loudly.
On the day of the procession, the strangers pretended to dress him in the new clothes.
The Emperor walked through the streets while all the people cheered.
No one wanted to admit that they could see nothing.
Then a little child cried, “But he has nothing on!”
The people whispered the truth, and the Emperor knew they were right.
